recipe.history:
Parmigiano-Reggiano is often called the King of Cheeses, and for once the hyperbole is genuinely justified by the historical record. This aged hard cheese has been produced in the Emilia-Romagna and Lombardy regions of northern Italy for at least nine hundred years — documentation from Cistercian and Benedictine monasteries dating to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries describes the production of a large, hard, long-aged cheese that matches the description of what we now call Parmigiano-Reggiano. The production zone is legally defined and tightly controlled under Italian and European DOP law: the milk must come from cows fed only grass and hay within the designated provinces of Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena, and parts of Bologna and Mantua. Each wheel is made from the raw evening milk, partially skimmed, combined with the full-fat morning milk, inoculated with whey starter from the previous day's production, and cooked with natural calf rennet. The wheels are then aged a minimum of twelve months and often well over twenty-four, their surfaces inspected by Consorzio testers who tap the wheel with a small hammer and listen for the difference between a properly aged interior and a flaw. The result of this medieval process, maintained across a millennium, is a cheese of extraordinary crystalline complexity — salty, nutty, fruity, long on the finish, and irreplaceable in the Italian kitchen.

The concept of parmigiana — breading and frying protein and baking it under tomato sauce and melted cheese — is itself a study in cultural migration. The dish is claimed with equal passion by Naples, Sicily, and by Italian-Americans, who developed their own robust versions of eggplant parmigiana and chicken parmigiana in the immigrant communities of New York, New Jersey, and Boston. The famous Chicken Parm hero sandwich — a breaded, fried cutlet under marinara and mozzarella on Italian bread — became one of the great sandwiches of the American Northeast and was always pointing, whether it knew it or not, toward its inevitable destiny as a burger. The parmigiana burger layers these techniques directly onto a beef patty: the patty is breaded and fried like a cutlet, ladled with house-made marinara, blanketed in mozzarella and Parmigiano, and served with crispy-edged bravado on a substantial roll.

There was a deli three blocks from where I grew up that sold chicken parms on Saturday mornings and the line ran out the door by eleven. I ate more of those sandwiches than I could count, standing over the counter with both hands and a stack of paper napkins, and I always thought the most important decision in any such sandwich was the quality of the breading on the cutlet — whether it was thick and bready and limp, or thin and shatteringly crisp. The thin crisp is the right answer. I apply that principle to this burger: the breadcrumb coating should be Panko-fine, press-thin, and fried quickly in hot oil so that it crackles when you bite through it, before you hit the juice and beef of the medium-rare interior beneath.

A medium-rare burger at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit presents a particular structural challenge in a parmigiana preparation because the breading and frying step necessarily adds heat to the exterior of the patty before the final melting step under the broiler. The solution is to begin with a very cold patty — refrigerator-cold, even briefly frozen on the exterior — sear a crust, bread immediately while the interior has received minimal heat, fry the breaded patty quickly just to set and color the crust, and then use the broiler only to melt the cheese rather than to continue cooking the patty. With an instant-read thermometer and attention, medium rare is entirely achievable in a parmigiana preparation, and the reward — a juicy, pink interior beneath a shattering crust under molten cheese and bright marinara — is one of the most extraordinary things you can put on a plate and call a burger. There is no version of this that works at well done. A well-done parmigiana burger is a dry disc under sauce, nothing more.
ingredients: One 28-oz can whole San Marzano tomatoes
For the parmigiana breading and frying:
2 large eggs, beaten with 2 tablespoons whole milk
Neutral oil for frying (enough to fill skillet 1/2 inch deep)
6 oz fresh mozzarella, sliced into rounds (or 6 oz low-moisture mozzarella, shredded)
Freshly cracked black pepper for finishing
instructions: 1. MAKE THE CIABATTA ROLLS — DAY BEFORE (wet dough, best made ahead): Combine yeast and warm water in a large bowl. Add warm milk and stir. Add bread flour, semolina, salt, and olive oil. Mix with a stiff spatula or wooden spoon until a shaggy, very wet dough forms — ciabatta dough is wetter than most.

2. Perform a series of stretch-and-fold cycles: with wet hands, stretch one side of the dough up and fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat. Do this 8 times per set, then let the dough rest 30 minutes. Repeat this stretch-and-fold process 3 more times over 2 hours total.
3. Cover tightly with plastic wrap and refrigerate overnight (12 to 16 hours).

4. Next day, turn dough onto a generously floured surface. It will be very loose. Dust the top with flour and gently shape into a rough rectangle without degassing more than necessary. Cut into 6 roughly equal rectangular portions. Transfer to parchment-lined baking sheet, dusting surfaces with flour to prevent sticking. Proof covered at room temperature 1 1/2 to 2 hours.

5. Preheat oven to 450°F (232°C) with a baking stone or steel if available. Bake rolls 15 to 18 minutes, creating steam by placing a pan of hot water on the bottom rack for the first 8 minutes. Remove steam pan. Continue baking until rolls are deep golden and hollow-sounding when tapped. Cool on a wire rack.

6. MAKE THE MARINARA: Heat olive oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add garlic and red pepper flakes and cook 2 to 3 minutes until garlic is fragrant and just beginning to turn golden. Add tomatoes, crushing them by hand into the pot as you add them. Add oregano, salt, and sugar. Simmer uncovered over medium-low heat 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thickened and concentrated. Remove from heat and stir in torn basil. Taste and adjust seasoning. Keep warm.

7. SET UP THE BREADING STATION: Arrange three shallow dishes in a line: flour seasoned with salt and pepper in the first, beaten egg mixture in the second, and Panko mixed with grated Parmigiano, oregano, garlic powder, salt, and pepper in the third.

8. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground veal. Season with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and oregano. Form into 6 flat patties, approximately 4 1/2 inches wide and 1/2 inch thick (slightly thinner than usual to ensure even cooking through the breading). Place on a parchment-lined tray and freeze for 15 minutes to firm up — cold patties bread better and cook more evenly.

9. BREAD THE PATTIES: Working one at a time, dredge each cold patty in seasoned flour, shaking off excess. Dip in egg mixture, letting excess drip off. Press firmly into the Panko-Parmigiano mixture on both sides, ensuring full, even coverage. Return to the parchment tray. Refrigerate 10 minutes to set the breading.
10. PREHEAT THE BROILER to high. Position an oven rack 6 inches below the broiler element.

11. FRY THE BREADED PATTIES: Pour neutral oil into a large heavy skillet to a depth of 1/2 inch. Heat to 350°F (175°C). Working in batches of 2 or 3, carefully lower breaded patties into the hot oil. Fry 2 to 2 1/2 minutes per side until the breading is deep golden brown and crisp. Transfer to a wire rack set over a baking sheet. Check internal temperature — target 125°F (52°C) at this stage; the patty will continue cooking briefly under the broiler.

12. BROIL WITH CHEESE: Transfer the wire rack and baking sheet to the oven. Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of marinara sauce over each fried patty. Place a round of fresh mozzarella over the marinara. Sprinkle with grated Parmigiano. Broil 2 to 3 minutes until cheese is melted, bubbly, and just beginning to brown in spots. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Remove from broiler and rest 2 minutes.
13. TOAST THE ROLLS: Split ciabatta rolls and brush cut sides lightly with olive oil. Toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds, or place under the broiler for 1 minute until golden.
14. ASSEMBLE: Spread a thin layer of additional warm marinara on the bottom bun. Carefully transfer a cheese-topped patty to the bottom bun.

15. Spoon a small additional amount of marinara over the cheese. Lay 2 fresh basil leaves on top. Drizzle lightly with extra virgin olive oil. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and a crack of black pepper. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
